```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", out.width = "100%", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
# The article downloads its prices from CoinMarketCap while it is built. The download is
# made here first, out of sight, so the chunks below get it from the disk cache, and
# without it the code is shown without its results instead of failing the build.
online <- tryCatch(
  !is.null(golemcrypto::get_history("Bitcoin (BTC)", as.Date("2013-04-29"))),
  error = function(e) FALSE
)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = online)
```

`r if (!online) "> The prices could not be downloaded when this page was built, so the code is shown without its results."`

The Volatility, Drawdowns and Seasonality tabs of the [golemcrypto app](https://sedzinfo-golemcrypto.share.connect.posit.cloud/) work the same way in R. An `_analysis()` function does the calculations, and its result goes to three functions:

- `_text()` sums it up in sentences, as the app does above its charts;
- `plot_` draws its chart;
- `_table()`, for drawdowns and seasonality, shows its numbers as a sortable table.

All three analyses compare the present with a coin's past, so pass them the whole history. [Price charts in R](golemcrypto.html) shows how to find coins and download their prices.

```{r history}
library(golemcrypto)
btc <- get_history("Bitcoin (BTC)", as.Date("2013-04-29"))
```

## Volatility

`volatility_analysis()` asks whether the volatility of the last 30 days, and the move of the last 2 days, are normal for the coin. It compares them with the coin's history and with a GARCH(1,1) model, and forecasts the next 7 days. It needs more than a year of history.

```{r volatility}
analysis <- volatility_analysis(btc)
volatility_text(analysis)$month
```

`volatility_text()` has two more parts, `$recent` for the last 2 days and `$forecast` for the next 7. The numbers behind the sentences are in the analysis, such as the forecast ranges of the next closes:

```{r forecast}
analysis$forecast$days
```

`plot_volatility()` draws three panels:

- the volatility of every 30-day period of the history, with its median and 95th percentile;
- each of the last 90 days, as its move in the standard deviations the GARCH model expected;
- the last 30 closes, followed by the forecast.

```{r plot-volatility, fig.height = 7}
plot_volatility(analysis)
```

`plot_forecast()` draws the lower panel on its own: the last 30 closes, then the median close of the next 7 days, with the ranges of the middle half and of 95% around it. Hover over the median line for the ranges of a day:

```{r plot-forecast}
plot_forecast(analysis)
```

The arguments of `volatility_analysis()` change the periods. For example, `month_days = 7` and `recent_days = 1` ask about the last week and the last day:

```{r volatility-week}
week <- volatility_analysis(btc, month_days = 7, recent_days = 1)
volatility_text(week)$month$headline
volatility_text(week)$recent$headline
```

`plot_volatility()` takes `days` for the days of the middle panel and `context_days` for the closes before the forecast, which `plot_forecast()` takes too. The length and the probability of the forecast are set in `volatility_analysis()`, with `forecast_days` and `level`. For example, the next 14 days with 90% ranges, after the last 60 closes:

```{r forecast-options}
two_weeks <- volatility_analysis(btc, forecast_days = 14, level = 0.9)
plot_forecast(two_weeks, context_days = 60)
```

## Drawdowns

`drawdown_analysis()` measures how far the coin is below its all-time high, and lists its earlier falls of 20% or more with how long they took to recover:

```{r drawdowns}
falls <- drawdown_analysis(btc)
drawdown_text(falls)$now
```

The falls are in `falls$episodes`, the deepest first. A fall that has not got back to its high yet is marked `ongoing`:

```{r episodes}
columns <- c("peak_date", "trough_date", "depth_pct", "recovery_date", "days_total", "ongoing")
head(falls$episodes[, columns])
```

`plot_drawdowns()` draws the close on a log scale with the all-time high so far, and under it the drawdown. The falls are shaded from their peak to their recovery, and their troughs are numbered by depth:

```{r plot-drawdowns, fig.height = 6}
plot_drawdowns(falls)
```

`drawdown_table()` shows the same falls as a sortable table:

```{r drawdown-table}
drawdown_table(falls)
```

To list smaller falls as well, lower `min_depth`, for example `drawdown_analysis(btc, min_depth = 10)`.

## Seasonality

`seasonality_analysis()` asks whether some periods bring better returns than others. The period is one of:

- `"day"`, the days of the week;
- `"week"`, the weeks of the year;
- `"month"`, the months;
- `"year"`, the years of the four-year halving cycle of Bitcoin.

A Kruskal-Wallis test then asks whether the differences could be chance.

```{r seasonality}
months <- seasonality_analysis(btc, "month")
text <- seasonality_text(months)
text$groups$headline
text$chance$headline
```

The `$points` of each part give the details, such as the p-value of the test and how many months it compared.

`plot_seasonality()` shows the mean return of each group, with the median as a diamond, and under it the share of returns above 0. Hover over a bar for all the numbers of its group:

```{r plot-seasonality}
plot_seasonality(months)
```

`seasonality_table()` shows the numbers as a table:

```{r seasonality-table}
seasonality_table(months)
```

The other periods work the same way, for example the days of the week:

```{r seasonality-day}
plot_seasonality(seasonality_analysis(btc, "day"))
```

## Dark mode and saving

Like the price charts, every `plot_` function takes `mode = "dark"` for a dark page. The charts are plotly objects, and the tables are DT tables, so `htmlwidgets::saveWidget()` saves any of them as a web page:

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(plot_drawdowns(falls), "drawdowns.html")
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(drawdown_table(falls), "drawdowns_table.html")
```
